meta.description: No, Leonardo da Vinci didn't say it. This is management writer Tom Peters, from his 1994 Chicago Tribune column on corporate strategy.

meta.ogDescription: Not Leonardo da Vinci. It's Tom Peters, from his 1994 Chicago Tribune column — a modern line pinned on a Renaissance name.

answer.label: Not Leonardo da Vinci — actually Tom Peters
answer.sourceLine: This is a modern management aphorism by Tom Peters, co-author of In Search of Excellence. Wikiquote’s sourced section traces it to his syndicated column “The Best Corporate Strategy? None, Of Course,” in the Chicago Tribune, 11 July 1994 ↗. Its vocabulary — competitors who “quickly copy” a hit — belongs to late-20th-century business, not to a 15th-century Florentine. Da Vinci never wrote it.

source.excerpt: Life is pretty simple: You do some stuff. Most fails. Some works. You do more of what works. If it works big, others quickly copy it. Then you do something else. The trick is the doing something else.
trail: Wikiquote lists the quote in its Tom Peters ↗ sourced section, citing his column “The Best Corporate Strategy? None, Of Course,” Chicago Tribune, 11 July 1994 ↗.
Quote-scraper sites such as AZQuotes ↗ print the same words under Leonardo da Vinci with no source — the classic profile of a fabricated attribution.
The wording itself dates the line: a 15th-century painter’s notebooks contain nothing about rivals who “quickly copy” a product that “works big.” This is corporate-strategy language.
source.excerptNote: The line is a compressed statement of Peters’ core theme — relentless experimentation, doubling down on what wins, and moving on before a hit gets commoditized.

author.bio: Thomas J. Peters is an American writer on business management, best known for co-authoring In Search of Excellence (1982) with Robert H. Waterman Jr. Through books and a widely syndicated newspaper column, he championed decentralization, customer obsession, and above all relentless experimentation. This quote distills that last theme: try many things, keep the winners, and keep moving.

misattribution.heading: How da Vinci got the credit
misattribution.intro: This is a textbook “magnet name” swap: a punchy modern business line gets re-pinned onto Leonardo da Vinci, whose fame lends instant gravitas. The genuine author is a living management writer.

items.why: Quote-scraper databases like AZQuotes ↗ print these words under da Vinci with no citation to any notebook, letter, or treatise. None of his surviving writings contain it, and its business idiom — rivals who “quickly copy” a hit — is anachronistic for c. 1500.

misattribution.truthLine: The real author is management writer Tom Peters, whose 1994 Chicago Tribune column is cited in Wikiquote’s sourced section ↗.

context.heading: Why the line resonates
lead: Peters built a career arguing that no fixed strategy survives contact with a fast-moving market. The quote’s punchline — “The trick is the doing something else” — captures his belief that the hard part isn’t finding a winner but leaving it behind before competitors erode the advantage.
Stripped of its author, the aphorism travels easily as generic wisdom, which is exactly how it drifted onto Leonardo da Vinci across inspirational-quote sites.
context.pull: You do more of what works — then the trick is doing something else.
